building.name: Kentucky Building Code
building.edition: 2018 Kentucky Building Code, Fourth Edition, February 2024 (the 2015 International Building Code with Kentucky amendments)
building.local_amendments_note: Kentucky's code is statewide and mandatory; a local government may not adopt or enforce another building code for commercial construction. Louisville Metro Code section 150.001(A) adopts the Kentucky Building Code 'in full'.
building.quote: Section 2. Building Code. The 2015 International Building shall be the mandatory state building code for all buildings constructed in Kentucky except that: (1) The Kentucky amendments in the 2018 Kentucky Building Code shall supersede any conflicting provision in the 2015 International Building Code [...] (b) "2018 Kentucky Building Code", Fourth Edition, February 2024. [...] eff. 12-3-2024.
building.second_quote: The Kentucky Building Code is a "mini/maxi" code, meaning that it is a statewide, uniform, mandatory building code and local governments shall not adopt or enforce any other building code governing commercial construction.
building.city_quote: The Kentucky Building Code, as promulgated in 815 KAR 7:120, and the Kentucky Residential Code, as promulgated in 815 KAR 7:125, by the Board of Housing, Buildings and Construction, Commonwealth of Kentucky, are hereby adopted in full as an ordinance of the Metro Government.
building.city_quote_note: Louisville Metro Code section 150.001(A). The American Legal page itself returns 403; the sentence is as returned in a web-search result for that page and matches the excerpts WebFetch returned from a secondary copy (https://www.zoneomics.com/code/louisville-KY/chapter_2). fixtures.basis: Louisville cannot amend the counts. The toilet-count chart is a state regulation (815 KAR 20:191), reached through Section 2902.1 of the Kentucky Building Code, which is statewide and which local governments may not replace; Metro Code section 150.001 adopts the Kentucky Building Code in full; and plumbing in Jefferson County is inspected by state plumbing inspectors. The excerpts of Metro Code Chapter 150 returned from a secondary copy contain no provision on restrooms or toilets. The state pack's worked examples stand.

permit.exempt_list_quote: 105.1 Required. Any owner or owner's authorized agent who intends to construct, enlarge, alter, repair, move, or change the occupancy of a building or structure, or to erect, install, enlarge, alter, repair, remove, convert, or replace any electrical, gas, mechanical, or plumbing system, the installation of which is regulated by this code, or to cause any such work to be performed, shall first make application to the building official and obtain the required permit. 105.2 Work exempt from permit. Exemptions from permit requirements of this code shall not be deemed to grant authorization for any work to be done in any manner in violation of the provisions of this code or any other laws or ordinances of this jurisdiction. Permits shall not be required for the following: Building: 1. One-story detached accessory structures used as tool and storage sheds, playhouses, and similar uses, provided the floor area is not greater than 120 square feet (11 m2). 2. Fences not over 7 feet (2134 mm) high. 3. Oil derricks. 4. Retaining walls that are not over 4 feet (1219 mm) in height measured from the bottom of the footing to the top of the wall, unless supporting a surcharge or impounding Class I, II, or IIIA liquids. 5. Water tanks supported directly on grade if the capacity is not greater than 5,000 gallons (18 925 L) and the ratio of height to diameter or width is not greater than 2:1. 6. Sidewalks and driveways not more than 30 inches (762 mm) above adjacent grade, and not over any basement or story below and are not part of an accessible route. 7. Painting, papering, tiling, carpeting, cabinets, counter tops, and similar finish work. 8. Temporary motion picture, television, and theater stage sets and scenery. 9. Tents and membrane structures having an area of 400 square feet (37 m2) or less. 10. Shade cloth structures constructed for nursery or agricultural purposes, not including service systems. 11. Swings and other playground equipment accessory to detached one- and two-family dwellings. 12. Window awnings in Group R-3 and U occupancies, supported by an exterior wall that do not project more than 54 inches (1372 mm) from the exterior wall and do not require additional support. 13. Non-fixed and movable fixtures, cases, racks, counters, and partitions not over 5 feet 9 inches (1753 mm) in height. [...] Plumbing: [...] 2. The clearing of stoppages or the repairing of leaks in pipes, valves, or fixtures, and the removal and reinstallation of water closets, provided such repairs do not involve or require the replacement or rearrangement of valves, pipes, or fixtures.
permit.partitions_named_note: The word 'partitions' appears in item 13, but only for non-fixed, movable ones not over 5 feet 9 inches high. Toilet partitions or compartments are not named, and they are fixed to the floor, wall or ceiling. Item 7 ends with 'similar finish work'. The list does not settle whether replacing or adding toilet partitions needs a permit.

page.meta: Commercial bathroom partitions delivered to Louisville job sites. Price your restroom, pick a material and see the Kentucky rules that apply here.
page.lead: Commercial bathroom partitions for Louisville distribution centers, hospitals and clinics, schools and restaurants, shipped by freight to your job site.
page.stall_bullet: - **How many stalls:** Kentucky's plumbing rules set the number of toilets and urinals by how many people use the building. They are the same statewide, Louisville can't change them, and state plumbing inspectors enforce them here. The table below shows what that means.
page.permit_bullet: - **Permits:** Louisville Metro Construction Review issues building permits in Louisville under Kentucky's statewide building rules, which require a permit to alter or repair a building unless the work is exempt. The exempt list covers "painting, papering, tiling, carpeting, cabinets, counter tops, and similar finish work" and movable partitions no taller than 5 feet 9 inches that aren't fixed in place. It doesn't name toilet partitions, so ask Construction Review (502-574-3321) whether your replacement needs one. You don't need a permit to buy partitions.
page.install_rule: Building permits in Louisville come from Louisville Metro Construction Review. A building contractor who takes out a permit there needs a Louisville Metro building contractor identification: Type A, or Type B for a single permit. Kentucky doesn't license general contractors at state level for work like partition installation. Ask Construction Review whether your installer needs the identification for a partition job. You don't need a permit to buy partitions.
page.faq_install_extra: A building contractor who takes out a permit in Louisville needs a Louisville Metro contractor identification.
page.public_jobs_bullet: - **Public jobs:** Kentucky repealed its wage law for public construction in 2017, so a set wage applies only on federally funded jobs, under the federal Davis-Bacon Act. For a carpenter on building work in Jefferson County that rate is $30.80 an hour plus $22.34 in benefits.
page.sales_tax_bullet: - **Sales tax:** 6% in Louisville, all of it Kentucky's state tax.
page.buyers_extra: - **Distilleries, breweries and event venues:** a finish that suits the visitor areas, in a material that stands up to tour and event crowds.

louisvilleky.gov and the Louisville Metro code library (American Legal) block automated access (403). The city's permit pages and Metro Code sections 150.001, 150.002, 150.083 and 150.084 were read only through search-result summaries and a secondary copy (Zoneomics): open them in a browser and check the wording, including the city's own list of commercial work that needs no permit.

The permit bullet quotes the Kentucky Building Code's exempt list, read on the state's own copy; search summaries say the city's commercial list repeats it and that the city calls its lists not exhaustive.

Schools, state-owned buildings and buildings above the local size limits (for example offices holding more than 100 people) are reviewed by the Kentucky Department of Housing, Buildings and Construction, not by Louisville Metro, unless Louisville has been given wider jurisdiction: confirm with Construction Review which office reviews a given job. The access bullet already says the state reviews larger buildings and all schools.

The city's site calls the office Construction Review; the Metro Code names the Department of Code and Regulations; the local-rules entry says Develop Louisville, Construction Review. Check the current department name in a browser.

Jeffersontown, listed among the nearby cities, runs its own building office (502-267-8333, per the state's Jefferson County sheet); Jeffersonville and New Albany are in Indiana, whose codes and sales tax were not researched for this page.
No Louisville Metro rule on single-user restroom signs or all-gender rooms was found; Metro Code Chapter 92 (civil rights) was not read. Confirm in a browser that it holds no restroom sign rule.
The date Kentucky's 6% rate began is not on the pages read, so the page gives no date.
The carpenter rate is the union rate CARP0175-001 dated June 1, 2025 in wage determination KY20260093, modification 1: recheck on sam.gov before launch, as a new modification may carry a newer rate.
Any Louisville Metro wage rule on city contracts was not looked for.
The four building types in the lead and the buyers bullet on distilleries, breweries and event venues are editorial, not sourced.
The stall table, its intro, the restroom bullet and the capacity sentence are the state pack's, unchanged: Louisville cannot amend them.
